questions.prompt: Which named ASR rule directly protects against the LSASS-access technique covered in Level 5's memory forensics content?
options: Block Office applications from creating child processes
Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)
Block executable content from email and webmail
Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content
questions.explanation: This rule exists specifically to stop the LSASS-access pattern that Level 5's LSASS memory analysis lesson covers from the artifact side -- ASR blocks it at the behavior level before it happens.

questions.prompt: An ASR rule fires in Audit mode rather than Block mode for a credential-theft attempt. What actually happened?
options: The attempt was fully blocked and prevented
The action was logged (Event ID 1122) but not actually stopped -- Audit mode provides visibility without prevention
Audit mode only applies to non-credential-related rules
questions.explanation: Audit mode logs what would have been blocked without stopping it. A 1122 event for a credential-theft rule is exactly as urgent as a 1121 (Block mode) event -- the only difference is the action wasn't actually prevented.

questions.prompt: Why is Tamper Protection specifically designed to resist changes from a local administrator account, not just a standard user?
options: Local administrators are never able to change any Windows settings
A compromised administrator account is one of the most common points an intrusion reaches, so Tamper Protection is built to resist exactly that threat model
Tamper Protection only applies to guest accounts
Administrator accounts are automatically trusted by all security products
questions.explanation: Local admin rights normally allow changing almost any security product's behavior. Tamper Protection is a deliberate exception, controlled by cloud-managed policy, precisely because attackers frequently do reach local admin during an intrusion.

questions.prompt: What does a 1121/1122 event immediately followed by a 5007 exclusion-added event for the same path suggest?
options: This is completely routine and requires no investigation
Someone hit a real ASR block or audit trigger, then engineered around it with an exclusion rather than reporting a false positive
The 5007 event is unrelated to the ASR event
This pattern only occurs during scheduled maintenance windows
questions.explanation: This sequence -- a real detection followed by a targeted exclusion for the same path -- suggests deliberate evasion of a control that just fired, rather than a legitimate false-positive resolution process.
